dailyRead: This is a Saturday page, so the useful work is not a price update - nothing trades until Monday's open - but a reckoning with the two events that were still ahead when yesterday's file was written, both of which have now resolved, and one of which reverses a call this page made three days ago. Take the yen first, because it is the simpler of the two. Yesterday's file named Ueda's press conference as the single thing that could reprice the yen complex, cut JPY from +1 to 0 on the published 7-2 vote split, and said explicitly that it stopped at 0 rather than -1 because 1.25% is genuine tightening and because 157 is the zone where the Ministry of Finance bought yen twelve days ago. The conference has now happened and it resolved on the dovish side of that hedge. Ueda raised the policy rate to a 31-year high and said the Bank stands ready to keep going, but he gave no explicit forward guidance on the pace, and with Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato having dissented AGAINST the increase, the market read the combination as a cap rather than a signal: the yen extended its losses through the conference and closed the week at 156.874, up 2.12% on the week against the dollar and lower for an eighth consecutive session. TE's own calendar is the corroborating fact here - it now carries 1.25% unchanged at the October 30 meeting, so on the canonical source there is no further hike scheduled inside the horizon this page trades, against a Fed sitting at 4.00% with sixteen of eighteen participants projecting at least one more increase. A currency whose central bank has just tightened into a 31-year high and still cannot hold a bid is telling you the carry gap is doing the work, so JPY goes to -1, JPYBASKET turns SHORT, and the XXX/JPY crosses go long against every currency scored above it. Two things keep the conviction on those tickets at LOW-MED rather than higher, and they should be read as position sizing rather than as doubt about the direction: the Ministry of Finance intervened at a better level than this less than a fortnight ago, and USD/JPY is still NEGATIVE on the month at -0.82%, which is not the profile of a one-way slide. The BoJ Summary of Opinions on September 30 is the next thing that can change it. The second item is the one that matters more, because it reverses this page rather than extending it. On Wednesday this file wrote that August CPI closed the hawkish route for sterling, that the two series the MPC targets had not moved - core steady at 2.6% for a fourth month, services steady at 3.4% - and that the only way back to +1 was services inflation above 3.4% in the September print. That framing was too narrow, and the evidence that it was too narrow arrived on Friday. Ofgem confirmed the energy price cap will rise 4% on October 1, to 1,723 pounds, with the GAS component up 8%, and attributed the increase directly to higher wholesale gas prices caused by the Middle East conflict - with a further 9% rise already forecast for Q1 2027. That is not a forecast of imported inflation, it is an administered price increase that is now scheduled. Underneath it the wholesale market went the same way: UK gas rose a third consecutive session, +3.90% to 198.16, which erased the entire weekly decline this page was tracking as a disinflationary offset - the week is now -0.05% against -1.87% yesterday and -6.08% on Wednesday - and left the month at +26.71%. Set that against what the MPC actually did on Thursday: it held at 3.75% with a 0/9 vote to cut and a 3/9 vote to HIKE, both TE-verified. Three members were already voting for 4% before the cap was confirmed. The correct reading of the reaction function is that this committee is energy-led, not core-led, and the September CPI test this page set was measuring the wrong series. GBP goes to +1. The invalidation has to be stated with the same specificity, because there is a real offset and it is easy to miss: the same Ofgem announcement cuts VAT on domestic electricity from 5% to ZERO between October 1 and March 31, which mechanically subtracts from measured October CPI and is worth roughly 45 pounds on the cap. So the headline that reaches the MPC on November 5 will be flattered downward by a tax change even as the underlying energy cost rises, and a committee that already said it looks through imported energy has been handed a reason to look through this too. That is why sterling goes to +1 and not higher, why every sterling ticket here is LOW-MED or MEDIUM and none is HIGH, and it is also why the cleanest expression of the view is not GBP/USD at all. It is EUR/GBP SHORT. Both economies are taking the identical gas shock - EU gas +4.14% and German gas +4.25% on Friday, both up about 25% on the month, UK gas +3.90% and +26.71% - and their central banks have publicly committed to opposite responses to it. The euro area's final August HICP revised DOWN to 3.2%, with services at 3.0% from 3.3% and core at 2.4%, so what is holding the euro headline up is energy at +14.3% y/y, and an import bill is what the ECB looks through; its next scheduled item is the October 8 accounts, with no decision until late October. Britain's committee has three members voting to hike on a confirmed administered energy increase. Same shock, opposite reaction function, and the cross at 0.85741 does not price the divergence. That is the trade of the week, and it does not depend on the dollar being right. Australia holds +2 and the case hardened rather than merely persisted. Bullock, Hauser, Hunter and Jones appeared before the House Standing Committee on Economics on Friday, and the message was not the balanced one the August minutes carried: Hauser said rates are only now closer to a sensible level of long-term real rates than they were a year or two ago, Bullock framed the open question as whether tightening to date is SUFFICIENT to return inflation to target in reasonable time, and Hauser pointed at an AI and tech boom that has repeatedly surprised the RBA's global growth forecasts to the upside. Markets have moved with them and now price a 70-75% chance of a hike on September 29. This is the one place on the page where the canonical source and the market disagree and the disagreement should be surfaced rather than smoothed: TE's calendar still carries 4.35% for September 29, unchanged, so the hike is a market view and not a forecast this page can attribute to TE. The honest position is that AUD is priced for a hawkish RBA and the risk is therefore asymmetric against it, which is why the Australian longs are expressed against the weakest legs - AUD/NZD, AUD/JPY, AUD/CAD, AUD/CHF - and why AUD/USD stays RANGE despite the rate differential about to move Australia's way. The specific test is Thursday at 01:30Z: the August labour force survey, consensus around +15K after July's -15.8K, with unemployment at 4.5% and participation slipping to 66.9%. A second negative employment print three business days before the board meets would take the hike pricing apart and AUD back to +1. Copper corroborates the Australian view from the physical side and it is the strongest structural story on the commodity board: 6.6150 and +2.25% on the week, after an LME record of 14,533 dollars a tonne on September 7, available LME stocks drained to roughly 90,000 tonnes, and cash trading more than 550 dollars over three-month futures - a backwardation last seen in 2021 - driven by tariff arbitrage pulling metal into US warehouses. Oil and the metals remain one trade and the mechanism is now explicit. WTI fell a third consecutive session to 100.300, -1.58%, and finished the week essentially flat at +0.25%, with Brent 103.870 and -0.71% on the week, because traders are weighting Saudi Arabia's workarounds more heavily than the fighting: crude is being loaded through Oman, ship-to-ship transfers near Sohar are running well above August levels, and roughly half the damaged East-West pipeline capacity is guided back within days. The falling energy premium pulls inflation expectations and real yields down, and the metals take it - gold 4383.45 and +0.76% on the week, silver 66.236 and +1.60% on the day for +3.07% on the week, the best performer on the board, with a sixth consecutive annual structural deficit now projected near 46 million ounces. But the geopolitical premium has NOT gone away and the page should not pretend it has: Hormuz is still running roughly 10 transits a day against a pre-crisis baseline of 88 to 130, war-risk premiums run 3 to 10 million dollars for a single transit of a 100 million dollar hull, Houthi attacks on Saudi facilities at Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait wounded 73 people this week, and Washington's ceasefire track has stalled even as Trump says the war is near its end. That is why USOIL stays RANGE and not SHORT, and why CAD stays at 0 rather than being cut: the Canadian dollar has no rate support with the BoC held at 2.25% through Oct 28 on TE's forecast, employment at -41,700 and services PMI at 46.8, but the terms-of-trade leg is a coin flip rather than a headwind. The franc is the quiet position ahead of the only scheduled event next week that this page is exposed to. CHF stays at 0 - USD/CHF is +3.11% on the month, so the haven bid is absent while crude falls - but Switzerland's data is better than a zero policy rate suggests, with GDP at 2.3% y/y, manufacturing PMI at 57.1 and CPI accelerating to 0.8% from 0.4%, and the SNB meets Thursday at 07:30Z. TE forecasts 0% and so does the economist consensus, so the rate is not the risk; Schlegel's conditional inflation forecast and his language on intervention are, and a franc-positive surprise there is the main threat to USD/CHF LONG and to the CHF-cross shorts. New Zealand stays last and the reasoning is unchanged and still correct. The RBNZ has hiked twice, to 2.75% on September 2, with Q2 inflation at 4.1%, and has said plainly that core inflation, wages and expectations are still consistent with a return to the 1-3% band by mid-2027 - it is looking through the fuel spike, which is the mirror image of the Bank of England and the reason this pair of currencies sits at opposite ends of the board. TE carries 2.75% unchanged at October 28. Underneath that, unemployment is 5.6% and rising, Q2 GDP slowed to +0.2% q/q, and the currency is the worst on the board at -1.58% on the week and -3.62% on the month. NZD/USD SHORT remains the widest score gap available at four points. The cleanest four things on the page: EUR/GBP short on the reaction-function split, NZD/USD short on the widest gap, AUD/NZD long, and silver. Nothing is HIGH conviction into a weekend with the RBA, the SNB and the Australian labour force survey all inside six days.

USD.note: TE re-verified: Fed funds upper bound 4.00%, raised from 3.75% on September 16, the first increase since 2023. Nothing in the five macro metrics changed this session - it is a Saturday and no US data has printed since Thursday - so this is a re-verification rather than an update, and the score rests on the same two pillars it did yesterday. First, the projections: TE's calendar carries Interest Rate Projection 1st Yr at 4.1% against 3.6% previously and 2nd Yr at 3.9% against 3.4%, press accounts put the 2026 median at 4.1% from 3.8% in June, and sixteen of eighteen participants project at least one further increase across October and December, with real GDP revised to 2.3%, unemployment to 4.1% and core PCE to 3.4%. Second, the growth leg, which was stress-tested on Thursday against a trigger this page wrote in advance and passed: the Philadelphia Fed index printed 37.8 against a 30.5 consensus and initial jobless claims FELL to 196,000 against a 208,000 consensus, with continuing claims at 1,730,000 and the four-week average at 203,000. The rest of the TE picture is unchanged: CPI 3.4% y/y with core easing to 2.4%, unemployment 4.1%, non-farm payrolls +162,000, retail sales +1.2% m/m with the control group +1.4%, services PMI 56.5, GDP annual growth 2.1%, core PCE annual 3.3%. One caution on sourcing: some sell-side commentary this weekend describes market pricing as heavily favouring an October hike. TE's own calendar does not - it carries 4% at October 28, an unchanged rate - and this page follows TE. The two genuine qualifiers also stand: Warsh said the Fed does not at this stage envisage an aggressive tightening cycle, and consumer confidence has fallen to 47.8 from 51.7. Next week's inputs are Goolsbee Monday, Williams, Jefferson and Barkin Tuesday, flash PMIs Wednesday and claims Thursday, with August core PCE at the end of the month the real test. What takes USD off +3: core PCE confirming the 2.4% core CPI deceleration rather than the 3.4% projection, or claims breaking back above 207K.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz transit counts, Saudi East-West pipeline repair and the stalled US-Iran ceasefire track
catalysts.note: The regime variable, and undated by nature. Hormuz is running roughly 10 transits a day against a pre-crisis baseline of 88 to 130, war-risk premiums are 3 to 10 million dollars for a single transit of a 100 million dollar hull, and Houthi strikes on Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait wounded 73 people this week. Against that, Saudi workarounds are working well enough to have pushed crude down three sessions. Every score on this board that involves energy - CAD, NOK-style terms of trade, GBP's cap, the euro's gas bill, CHF's haven bid, the metals - resolves through this.

geopolitics: The transmission chain this week ran in two directions at once, and separating them is the most useful thing on this page. On the crude leg the premium drained: WTI fell a third consecutive session to 100.300, -1.58%, finishing the week essentially flat at +0.25%, with Brent 103.870 and -0.71% on the week. That happened despite the fighting escalating, not because it eased - Houthi forces struck Saudi facilities at Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait, wounding 73 people and forcing temporary halts, while Washington's ceasefire track stalled even as Trump said the war is near its end and claimed direct talks with Tehran. What moved the price was supply logistics: Saudi Arabia is loading more crude through Oman, ship-to-ship transfers near Sohar are running well above August levels, and the kingdom has guided that roughly half the damaged East-West pipeline capacity returns within days with full operations inside six weeks. Traders weighted the workaround above the war. The physical chokepoint has NOT reopened, and that is the part to keep on the page: Hormuz is running about 10 transits a day against a pre-crisis baseline of 88 to 130, and war-risk premiums run 3 to 10 million dollars for a single transit of a 100 million dollar hull before cargo cover. So crude is cheaper while the risk is unchanged, which is an unstable equilibrium rather than a resolution - it is why USOIL is RANGE with an upward asymmetry and why CAD stays at 0 rather than being cut. On the gas leg the premium went the other way and this is where the FX consequences are cleanest. EU gas rose 4.14% to 79.52, German gas 4.25% to 80.54 and UK gas 3.90% to 198.16, all three erasing the weekly declines this page had been tracking as a disinflationary offset, and all three sitting about 25% higher on the month. Gas does not travel like crude; it cannot be rerouted on shuttle tankers, so the European energy bill is still rising while the oil price falls. The FX read follows directly from how the two European central banks have committed to treat that. Britain's is going to respond: Ofgem confirmed the October 1 cap rise at 4% with the gas component up 8%, blamed explicitly on the Middle East conflict, and three of nine MPC members were already voting for 4%.
